module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 453

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/453](https://www.erdosproblems.com/453)
- [Er70b] Erdős, P., *Some applications of graph theory to number theory*. Proc. Second Chapel Hill
  Conf. on Combinatorial Mathematics and its Applications (Univ. North Carolina, Chapel Hill, N.C.,
  1970) (1970), 136-145.
- [Er74b] Erdős, P., *Remarks on some problems in number theory*. Math. Balkanica (1974), 197-202.
- [Er77c] Erdős, Paul, *Problems and results on combinatorial number theory. III*. Number theory day
  (Proc. Conf., Rockefeller Univ., New York, 1976) (1977), 43-72.
- [Er80] Erdős, Paul, *A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory*. Ann. Discrete Math.
  (1980), 89-115.
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., *Unsolved problems in number theory*. (2004), xviii+437.
- [Po79] Pomerance, Carl, *The prime number graph*. Math. Comp. (1979), 399-408.
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos453

/-- The eventual prime inequality asked in Erdős Problem 453, using Mathlib's zero-based primes. -/
def EventuallyHasPrimeWitness : Prop :=
  ∃ N : ℕ, ∀ n : ℕ, N ≤ n →
    ∃ i : ℕ, i < n ∧
      (Nat.nth Nat.Prime n) ^ (2 : ℕ) <
        Nat.nth Nat.Prime (n + i) * Nat.nth Nat.Prime (n - i)

/--
Is it true that, for all sufficiently large $n$, there exists some $i<n$ such that
$$
p_n^2 < p_{n+i}p_{n-i},
$$
where $p_k$ is the $k$th prime?

Pomerance proved that the answer is no.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos453.lean"]
theorem erdos_453 : answer(False) ↔ EventuallyHasPrimeWitness := by
  sorry

end Erdos453

findings.description: The module's [Er74b] reference (line 28) identifies “Remarks on some problems in number theory,” pp. 197–202, but the relevant 1974 question occurs in the separately headed contribution “Problems,” pp. 203–204, §4.33.2.I. Both contributions are included in the same archive PDF, which likely explains the citation slip. The Lean mathematics is unaffected.
findings.source_evidence: https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1974-27.pdf distinguishes “4.32 (1974) 197–202 — Remarks on some problems in number theory” from “4.33 (1974) 203–204 — Problems.” On p. 203, §4.33.2.I asks whether infinitely many primes p_k satisfy p_k² > p_{k+i}p_{k-i} for every i < k.
findings.suggested_fix: Cite Erdős, P., “Problems,” Math. Balkanica 4 (1974), 203–204, specifically §4.33.2.I, or explicitly include this accompanying contribution in the reference.

reformulations.difference: The source uses one-based primes P₁ = 2 and positive witnesses i < m. Writing q(n) = Nat.nth Nat.Prime n = P_{n+1}, a literal reindexing permits 0 < i ≤ n. The file instead permits i = 0 and requires i < n, thus omitting the endpoint i = n.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The strict inequality rules out i = 0 automatically. At the other endpoint the product is q(2n)q(0) = 2q(2n), which is at most q(n)² for all sufficiently large n by standard elementary prime-growth estimates. Hence this endpoint cannot provide an eventual witness either. Enlarging the cutoff and reindexing m = n + 1 gives both implications. This was proved in /workspace/review/index-equivalence.lean as IndexReview453.full_source_iff, using a separately proved eventual endpoint bound and only prime-growth lemmas, not the solution of problem 453. Its axioms are only propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound.

review.notes: Both declarations are mathematically faithful. Pomerance's paper explicitly states the original eventual-existence question and proves its negative answer, agreeing with answer(False) and research solved. Scratch checks verified small cases, redundant witness positivity, and the negated quantifiers. The external proof and an adapter to the exact repository statement were kernel-checked after four simplifier-only compatibility edits in a scratch copy for Lean 4.33.1; neither depends on sorryAx or custom axioms. The live Erdős Problems page returned HTTP 403 despite descriptive User-Agent headers, so the question and resolution were independently checked against the primary literature. The reviewed file was not modified.
